channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Greenpeace estimates extreme heat and drought will cost the German economy at least EUR 36 billion, around 0.8-0.9% of output, while a tornado struck Hesse, Typhoon Narra flooded China's Guangxi and haze from Indonesian fires choked Southeast Asia.
item.description:
The season's physical-climate toll is mounting and quantifiable. Greenpeace estimates that extreme heat and weeks of drought will cost the German economy at least EUR 36 billion — equivalent to 0.8-0.9% of output — counting crop failures, forest fires, health costs, and productivity and education losses, and it urged the federal cabinet to treat the climate crisis with "the necessary seriousness." In Bavaria, trees are shedding leaves early as a survival response, weakening them for years. A tornado swept the greater Wetzlar area of Hesse, damaging dozens of houses and causing estimated damages in the millions in Solms alone. In China, Typhoon Narra forced the evacuation of 54,000 people amid flooding in Guangxi, and cross-border haze from forest fires in Indonesia's Sumatra and Kalimantan pushed regional air quality to among the worst in the world.

Industry Impact

Physical-climate shocks hit the ACS industry through demand, logistics and raw materials. Drought that lowers river levels disrupts the barge logistics German chemical producers rely on and raises the cost of moving inputs and finished goods, while crop failures feed into bio-based feedstock availability and prices. Storms and floods in China and Southeast Asia disrupt manufacturing and construction — key ACS end-markets — and can interrupt supplier operations and shipping in the region. A quantified EUR 36 billion hit to Germany also reinforces the competitiveness pressures its industry is already flagging. ACS planners should treat weather-driven logistics and feedstock volatility as a recurring, not exceptional, planning factor.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | The Economic Times | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: New-energy vehicles topped 60% of monthly new-car sales in China in July for the first time, with cumulative share above 50%, as car exports hit a half-year record of 5.1 million and Beijing drafted self-driving liability rules.
item.description:
China's auto transition crossed two thresholds at once. The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said new-energy vehicles (battery-electric and plug-in hybrids) accounted for over 60% of monthly new-vehicle sales in July for the first time, and more than 50% of cumulative sales year-to-date; NEVs took nine of the ten best-selling passenger models, and three Chinese carmakers entered the global top ten brands in the first half. Exports set a half-year record of 5.096 million vehicles, led by Chery and BYD. On the regulatory side, the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress gave a first reading to a draft amendment of the Road Traffic Safety Law that, for the first time in Chinese law, defines autonomous and assisted-driving functions and clarifies liability when a self-driving function is active at the time of a violation.

Industry Impact

Autos are among the largest end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants, and an NEV-dominated, export-leading Chinese fleet steers that demand toward battery bonding and thermal management, lightweight structural adhesives and EV-specific coatings — a materials mix distinct from combustion vehicles. Record exports mean China-made cars, and the ACS content in them, are increasingly shipped worldwide, extending Chinese material specifications into export markets. The self-driving liability draft signals a maturing regulatory framework around autonomous vehicles that will shape sensor housings, bonding and protective coatings for driver-assistance hardware. ACS suppliers to the automotive sector should prioritise EV- and NEV-oriented product lines and track China's fast-moving vehicle regulations.

People's Daily Online | Commercial Times | Wallstreet Online

item.title: Unitree raised CNY 6.1 billion in a heavily oversubscribed Shanghai IPO, the first humanoid-robot maker on a mainland exchange, as reports show 97 of every 100 humanoid robots shipped worldwide in the first half were made in China.
item.description:
China's robotics build-out reached a financial milestone. Unitree Robotics raised CNY 6.1 billion (about USD 850 million) in its Shanghai listing — the first humanoid-robot manufacturer on a mainland Chinese exchange — in an offering oversubscribed by retail investors more than 8,000 times, a record for the STAR Market; the shares opened up more than 600% and settled around a 460% gain. The scale of China's lead is striking: an industry report says 97 of every 100 humanoid robots shipped worldwide in the first half of 2026 were "Made in China," with the country shipping more than 40,000 units. Beijing is also institutionalising the sector, with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology drafting a national humanoid-robot standards system and a stated goal of at least 100 key standards by 2028.

Industry Impact

A capital-rich, standards-backed Chinese robotics sector is both an opportunity and a competitive signal for the ACS industry. Humanoid and industrial robots use structural adhesives, thermal-interface materials, protective coatings and sealants in their assembly, so a scaling Chinese fleet expands demand for those specialty materials — increasingly specified to Chinese national standards that ACS suppliers will need to meet. At the same time, robot-dense manufacturing reshapes how ACS products are applied on customers' lines, favouring materials engineered for automated dispensing and bonding. Suppliers should track China's emerging robot standards and position specialty adhesive and coating portfolios for both robot makers and increasingly automated production environments.

Forbes | Xinhua Daily | Xinhua

item.title: The European Commission issued ten guidance documents for the definitive phase of its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the EU's import carbon levy, as tightening PFAS restrictions and new litigation add pressure on chemical and coatings makers.
item.description:
The EU's chemical rulebook tightened on two fronts. The Commission released ten guidance documents to help non-EU operators comply with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) in its definitive period — the phase that brings monitoring, reporting and financial obligations for importers of carbon-intensive goods, aimed especially at operators of installations outside the EU that make CBAM-covered products. Separately, pressure on "forever chemicals" is intensifying: the export body CHEMEXCIL is running a session to help exporters navigate evolving PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) restrictions and global regulatory trends, while ClientEarth lawyer Hélène Duguy is pursuing legal action against chemical manufacturers over PFAS pollution and challenging the EU's reapproval of the pesticide glyphosate. Together they mark a continued regulatory ratchet on carbon costs and chemical substances entering or made in the EU.

Industry Impact

Both threads land directly on the ACS industry. CBAM raises the administrative and eventual cost burden on carbon-intensive imported inputs — resins, intermediates and raw materials — that adhesives, coatings and sealants formulators rely on, and demands supplier-level emissions data that many non-EU producers are not yet set up to provide. PFAS restrictions bear on fluoropolymer-based and specialty formulations used in coatings and sealants, and rising litigation signals legal as well as regulatory exposure. ACS producers should map which inputs fall under CBAM, secure emissions documentation from suppliers now, and audit formulations for PFAS reliance ahead of tighter limits.

British Stainless Steel Association | CHEMEXCIL | The Guardian

item.title: GDP growth in the OECD area picked up to 0.5% in the second quarter of 2026 from 0.4%, with 27 of 30 reporting countries growing and Spain leading the major economies at 0.7%, even as G7 growth slowed to 0.3% on a weaker Germany.
item.description:
The developed-economy backdrop firmed modestly. The OECD's provisional estimates show area-wide GDP rising 0.5% quarter-on-quarter, a second straight quarter of acceleration that lifts the year-on-year rate to 2.7% from 2.3% at the start of the year. Growth was broad but uneven: 27 of the 30 countries with data expanded and three were flat. Spain again topped the major economies with a 0.7% rebound, comfortably above the OECD average and the eurozone. The G7 was the soft spot, slowing to 0.3% as Germany cooled from 0.4% to 0.2% and Italy also eased. The overall message is one of steady, if unspectacular, expansion across the rich world rather than a stall.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers, a developed-world growing at around half a percent a quarter means end-market demand keeps expanding but slowly, so volume plans should assume steady rather than accelerating industrial activity. The divergence matters more than the average: Spain and other faster movers offer relative upside, while a Germany decelerating to 0.2% underlines why the country's own industry is pressing for reform (see the German insight in this alert). ACS suppliers should weight capacity and commercial focus toward the faster-growing OECD markets while planning conservatively for the large but sluggish German and Italian bases.

OECD | El País

item.title: Russia rejected Ukraine's proposed Black Sea truce protecting grain ships and ordered the annexation of Donetsk by year-end, keeping over a quarter of world wheat exports exposed as the EU's Kaja Kallas readies a third more Russia sanctions.
item.description:
The war's economic front hardened again. President Zelenskyy said Ukraine offered to stop attacking ships carrying agricultural goods through the Black Sea, but Russia rejected the proposal, demanding in return that Ukraine guarantee not to strike Russian energy infrastructure — the two countries together account for more than 25% of global wheat exports. President Putin separately ordered the annexation of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region before year-end, and Zelenskyy warned Russia could mobilise a further 300,000 troops. On the Western side, EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas announced plans to raise the number of sanctioned Russian individuals, companies and organisations by around a third, as Moscow's economy and military recruitment strain; Putin, meanwhile, touted growing Russia–India trade in energy, fertilizers and nuclear power as a counterweight.

Industry Impact

The most direct channel for chemicals and ACS is agriculture and energy: a rejected Black Sea truce keeps grain-shipping and, by extension, food-price and fertilizer-market risk elevated, and any renewed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure would feed back into European gas and feedstock prices. A further round of EU sanctions widens the compliance perimeter for any firm with residual Russia-linked suppliers or logistics, while deeper Russia–India commodity ties hint at how displaced flows of energy and fertilizers may be rerouted. ACS producers should treat Black Sea and European energy volatility as a persistent input-cost risk into the autumn rather than a resolving one.

Lianhe Zaobao | Chinatimes | Frankfurter Rundschau | Anadolu Agency

item.title: India is negotiating free-trade deals with eight to nine more blocs to cover about 75% of global trade, including a Gulf pact and a USD 100 billion trade target with Russia, even as first-quarter growth is seen cooling to a four-quarter low near 7.1%.
item.description:
New Delhi is diversifying its trade relationships well beyond the near-complete US deal. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said India is in talks with at least eight to nine more groups of countries — together worth another USD 15 trillion of GDP — with the aim that its FTAs eventually cover around 75% of global trade; India has signed nine such agreements in four years. Talks on a free-trade deal with the Gulf Cooperation Council, India's largest trading-partner bloc, are advancing toward a ministerial meeting next month. In Moscow, External Affairs Minister Jaishankar and President Putin set a USD 100 billion bilateral-trade target by 2030, spanning energy, fertilizers and nuclear power, and India also lifted its ban on wheat and wheat-flour exports. Against this, a Reuters poll expects April–June growth eased to about 7.1%, a four-quarter low, on softer private investment and a delayed monsoon, with official figures due 31 August.

Industry Impact

India remains a structural growth market for the construction, automotive and consumer-manufacturing demand that pulls through adhesives, coatings and sealants, and a wider web of trade deals lowers tariff risk on the inputs and finished goods that flow through it. A GCC agreement and deeper India–Russia ties could reshape where chemical feedstocks and fertilizers are sourced, while the lifted wheat-export ban signals a more open trade stance. The cooling first-quarter growth is a reminder that the demand ramp is not linear, but the direction — more trade lanes, more predictability — supports the medium-term investment case for ACS capacity in India even as North American and China routes get harder.

Business Standard | The Economic Times | LiveMint | MarketScreener | DNA

item.title: German first-half GDP ran nearly 1% above a year earlier, but with insolvencies at a multi-year high the chemical association VCI and machinery makers are pressing Chancellor Merz for a growth turnaround on energy, taxes and bureaucracy.
item.description:
The German picture is improving at the top line but strained underneath. The Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported that first-half 2026 GDP, adjusted for prices, seasons and calendar effects, was nearly 1% above the previous year — yet flagged high energy prices, heavy bureaucracy, elevated company costs and skilled-labour shortages as drags on competitiveness, with insolvencies reaching 12,900 in the first half, the highest in years. The VCI, Germany's chemical industry association, called on the government to send a "clear signal" for growth: competitive energy prices and a reformed EU emissions-trading system, lower taxes and non-wage labour costs, a reset of the income-tax reform, and genuine cuts to bureaucracy. The machinery lobby VDMA offered a brighter note, with its valve segment expecting a second-half recovery led by pharmaceuticals, shipbuilding, energy and defence, while Switzerland's Swissmem warned the US tariff war cut mechanical, electrical and metal exports further.

Industry Impact

Germany is the core European market for industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants, so the VCI's intervention is a direct read on ACS demand conditions: the chemical sector itself judges current energy costs, taxes and red tape as growth-limiting, even as headline GDP inches up. A genuine reform push on energy and emissions trading would ease the input-cost pressure ACS producers share with their industrial customers, while the VDMA's expected second-half machinery recovery — and defence demand — points to selective volume upside. The practical read is cautious: treat the GDP uptick as fragile and cost-driven, and watch whether Merz's cabinet converts reform pledges into measures the chemical industry says it needs.

Frankfurter Rundschau | VCI | VDMA | Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: The European Commission is assembling a car-industry alliance with the UK, Japan and South Korea against Chinese overcapacity, as Goldman Sachs estimates existing and proposed EU measures could cover about 27% of China's exports to the EU.
item.description:
Europe's response to China is broadening from single-product duties to a coordinated bloc. Handelsblatt reports the Commission is working on a new alliance with Britain, Japan and South Korea, all of which face the same flood of Chinese exports; Bernd Lange, who chairs the European Parliament's trade committee, cited illegal subsidies, the resulting overcapacity and yuan undervaluation as shared problems. This follows the debate over tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars and a China goods deficit running above EUR 1 billion a day. Goldman Sachs economists estimate that existing and proposed EU trade measures could cover roughly 27% of China's annual exports to the EU — though they caution the scope of restrictions does not translate one-for-one into export losses, and the real impact depends on final policy detail. The EU absorbed 15% of China's exports last year, and those flows have kept rising, making this an increasingly prominent policy risk.

Industry Impact

A structural EU turn toward trade defence reshapes the competitive map for chemical and ACS producers on two fronts. Measures on Chinese vehicles alter volumes and sourcing across the automotive supply chain — a core ACS end-market — and a bloc-wide alliance raises the odds of Chinese retaliation that could catch European chemical exporters. More broadly, the prospect that measures touch a quarter or more of China's EU-bound goods signals rising input-cost volatility and shifting trade lanes. ACS suppliers should track which product categories the Commission and its new partners target, and prepare for a more fragmented, tariff-shaped Europe–Asia trade relationship.

Handelsblatt | Commercial Times

item.title: Washington is reportedly weighing a 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods over excess capacity, timed just before the expected Trump–Xi summit in September and lifting the Trump-era additional tariff rate on China back toward 20%.
item.description:
A fresh front on China is taking shape alongside the Canada fight. Bloomberg-cited sources say the administration is weighing an extra 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods, justified by China's excess capacity and export flood, ahead of a planned meeting between Presidents Trump and Xi in September. One option under discussion is to announce higher headline tariffs but postpone part of them, leaving a real effective rate around 7.5%; the numbers are not final and Trump may adjust before any announcement. If implemented, it would push the additional tariff rate imposed during Trump's second term back to roughly 20%, close to the agreed ceiling. In parallel, the US State Department pledged an "America first" approach at APEC talks being held in China weeks before Xi's US visit, underscoring that the tariff signal and the summit diplomacy are running at the same time.

Industry Impact

A 7.5% layer on Chinese goods would feed directly into the landed cost of chemical intermediates, additives and finished ACS inputs that still flow from China, and any Chinese retaliation could catch Western exporters. Because the measure is being floated right before a leaders' summit, its main signal is uncertainty: the effective rate, timing and product scope are all still moving. ACS producers sourcing from or selling into China should treat a further US–China tariff step as a live scenario in cost and sourcing plans, and watch the summit for whether the two sides ease or harden — the outcome will shape input prices and competitive dynamics well beyond this one rate.

Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | South China Morning Post

item.title: The US sanctioned nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels and widened its secondary-sanctions threat on countries trading with Iran, but held back the heaviest penalties and spared Chinese banks as Tehran threatened the Gulf.
item.description:
The "economic D-Day" proved to be a framework and a warning rather than a maximum blow. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced sanctions on close to 60 individuals, entities and vessels tied to Iran's nuclear, missile, cyber and oil networks, suspended general licenses that had allowed some transfers, and named five foreign-revenue sources — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping — as targets for future secondary sanctions. Crucially, the package did not name the Chinese banks suspected of handling Iran's oil trade, and the administration signalled it would give countries defined timelines to cut ties rather than impose the harshest measures immediately. President Trump insisted Iran is "completely collapsing," while Foreign Minister Araqchi dismissed the move as desperation. Tehran threatened a military response and further cuts to Gulf oil exports, and China's foreign ministry said Beijing would do "what is necessary" to protect its interests. Oil prices eased as traders read the announcement as less severe than feared.

Industry Impact

For the ACS industry the immediate feedstock risk is lower than a full embargo would imply, since oil prices softened and the toughest penalties were deferred — a modest relief for the energy and petrochemical inputs beneath adhesives, coatings and sealants. The lasting exposure is compliance rather than price: the widened secondary-sanctions net and the five named sectors mean customers, suppliers, insurers or shipping partners with Iran links can be placed off-limits on a defined timeline, so screening and contract clauses need tightening now. The decision to spare Chinese banks lowers the odds of an immediate US–China rupture over enforcement, but leaves that risk live for firms exposed to both markets.

Wirtschaftswoche | The Straits Times | The Economic Times | Global Times | The Nation

item.title: New 50% US tariffs on about USD 28 billion of Canadian goods took effect, and Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50% from January 2027 as Ottawa prepares for a prolonged trade war.
item.description:
The dispute moved from a broad tariff to a targeted assault on Canada's core industries. After trade talks collapsed, Washington used Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act — a rarely invoked provision allowing tariffs against countries deemed to discriminate against US commerce — to put 50% duties on roughly USD 28 billion of Canadian goods. Trump then said on Truth Social that tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel will rise to 50% from 1 January 2027, while US-made content stays at zero. Prime Minister Mark Carney called the relationship effectively "at war," rejected what he termed US demands for "subordination," and — according to officials — expects no return to talks before the US midterm elections, so his government is preparing a domestic aid package to ride out Trump's term. Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliation begins on 8 September, Ontario's Doug Ford is urging curbs on commodity exports such as electricity, potash and energy, and Carney has also framed the fight as protecting the French language and Quebec culture.

Industry Impact

This is now the central near-term risk for chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers with North American operations. The Canadian Coatings Association has warned that the tariffs hit about USD 28 billion of goods on top of sectoral duties that have already disrupted the coatings, adhesives, sealants and elastomers (CASE) sector for over a year, and it is urging both governments to de-escalate. A jump to 50% on autos and steel would raise input costs across the automotive and construction value chains that ACS suppliers serve on both sides of the border, and a fight that stretches past the midterms removes any near-term planning certainty. Firms should map exposure on both tariff lists, build in contract and pricing flexibility, and watch Canadian commodity-export threats that could reach potash and energy inputs.

BNN Bloomberg | The Economic Times | Fortune | Financial Post | MarketScreener | PCI Magazine
